title: A workflow for coordinating O-LCA and SO-LCA: a pilot study in ceramic manufacturing
Sliding scales in the steel industry – an effective basis for comparison?
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The decarbonization of the steel industry is an important contributor to reaching net-zero by 2050. Increased circularity is expected to aid in this transition. However, the constrained nature of scrap supply is often not accounted for, which could lead to unsustainable decision-making. A sliding scale framework could enable a more robust comparison between decarbonization measures. However, multiple frameworks have been developed, differing in their methodological approaches.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Method</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A four step method was implemented to investigate three sliding scale frameworks. This consisted of a literature review, comparative analysis, life cycle assessment, and discussion and recommendation development. In the first two phases the method documents of sliding scale frameworks were studied and compared based on a selection of fundamental elements and modelling requirements. For each framework, nine life cycle assessment scenarios were developed, according to the different methodological requirements of the respective system. These scenarios depict varying stages of conventional and decarbonized production across major production pathways. Finally, the results of the comparative analysis and LCA have been discussed, to determine if sliding-scale frameworks offer a robust basis for comparison, and to provide recommendations for future harmonization efforts between different frameworks.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The comparative analysis identified methodological differences for every investigated aspect. The influence of these differences on the LCA results is in the same order of magnitude as those brought on by technical decarbonization measures. While the sliding scale systems enable a comparison across different scenarios, different conclusions can be drawn depending on which system is chosen for the analysis. This is mainly due to how quantitative emission thresholds are derived, in addition to diverging definitions of low-emission steel production.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Harmonization is required for multiple elements of the sliding scale methodologies. Most importantly, the near-zero production definition should be refined to include additional quantitative criteria and a common definition of low-emission production is required. Furthermore, a uniform approach is required for determining quantitative emission thresholds. It is proposed that both near-zero and low-emission steel definitions be based on a reference installation threshold representing conventional production processes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Rethinking environmental comparison in advanced ceramics processing through life cycle assessment
Evaluating distributed construction with life cycle assessment: a scenario-based comparative study of construction-stage environmental impacts
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Distributed construction (DC) decentralizes fabrication and assembly across multiple locations while planning and coordination remain centralized. Empirical data on its construction-stage greenhouse gas impacts relative to conventional construction and traditional modular construction are limited. This study addresses this gap by providing a scenario-based comparative life cycle assessment of DC’s construction-stage environmental performance using a U.S. hospitality project.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study develops an attributional, comparative evaluation of life cycle greenhouse gas emissions (GHG) for a newly built hotel in Alpharetta, Georgia. The study evaluates three construction and production configurations: conventional construction (CC), traditional modular construction (TM), and a modeled distributed construction (DC) scenario that differs from TM mainly in its production and logistics network. The functional unit is the complete hotel project, with results also normalized per guestroom and per unit floor area. The system boundary follows EN 15978 production and construction stages A1–A5 and includes material production, transportation, construction energy and water use, and material impacts associated with construction waste. Scenario development draws on project documentation, published literature, industry presentations, professional meetings, and explicitly documented scenario assumptions. Sensitivity analysis examines key assumptions, including transport distance, facility proximity, payload and backhaul treatment, material-loss factors, construction duration, and energy intensity.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results and discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Under the modeled assumptions, the DC scenario has the lowest modeled construction-stage A1–A5 GHG emissions among the three scenarios. Total A1–A5 emissions are approximately 1,168 t CO₂e for CC, 1,055 t CO₂e for TM, and 1,004 t CO₂e for DC, representing estimated reductions of 14% relative to CC and 5% relative to TM. DC’s incremental advantage over TM mainly comes from lower transportation and construction energy- and water-related impacts. Modeled material impacts are identical for TM and DC and about 8% higher than for CC because of the double-layer module walls, and DC waste-associated impacts are slightly higher than TM because of the additional kitting-stage loss. The advantage relative to CC depends strongly on the assumed CC site material-loss factor; TM no longer has lower emissions than CC when the CC site loss falls below approximately 15%. Sensitivity analysis indicates that transportation performance depends heavily on facility proximity; under the current route, payload, and return-trip assumptions, DC transportation emissions reach parity with TM at a Rapid Plant-to-site distance of approximately 178 miles (287 km). These results are scenario-dependent: DC remains below TM across the other tested parameter ranges, but the advantage disappears when the Rapid Plant is more than approximately 245 mi (395 km) from the site or the Kit Center loss exceeds approximately 13%.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Distributed construction may achieve lower modeled construction-stage A1–A5 GHG emissions when localized fabrication and coordinated logistics are feasible. This study applies a comparative LCA framework to evaluate production-network configuration as an environmental performance variable in construction. The results indicate that any benefit depends on project-specific logistics and resource-use characteristics.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Comparative parametric life cycle assessment of NMC811 and NMC622 lithium-ion battery cells under varying recycled cathode metal content
Fleet-level prospective life cycle assessment: a scoping review of methods and standards toward harmonized modelling
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Life cycle assessment (LCA) is increasingly applied to evaluate long-term decarbonization pathways, e.g., in the automotive sector. While life cycle-based approaches are well established at product level, methodological concepts for prospective, fleet-level applications remain fragmented across scientific literature, standards, and policy frameworks. The purpose of this review is to systematically identify, structure, and synthesize methodological building blocks relevant to fleet-level prospective LCA (pLCA) of passenger vehicles and to assess existing gaps and harmonization potential.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A scoping review was conducted following PRISMA-ScR principles. Peer-reviewed literature from the period 2015–2025 was systematically identified through Scopus and Web of Science and supplemented by standards, methodological guidelines, and EU regulatory documents. In total, 44 documents were identified through the systematic search. An additional 19 applied assessments, policy studies, and corporate reports were included through purposive screening, resulting in a total of 63 documents. The documents were synthesized using a concept-driven clustering approach and organized into five methodological clusters: policy and normative frameworks, core methodological foundations, fleet- and system-level modelling, foreground technology modelling and upscaling, and scenario design with background system coupling. In addition, the 19 purposively selected sources and three sources from the systematic corpus were coded according to how they operationalize the fleet.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results and discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Most methodological elements are individually well established, yet they are not integrated in a consistent manner. The coding indicates that quantitative fleet-level results are presented using a common terminology, although they refer to at least three reference quantities that cannot be converted into one another: cohort-lifetime, stock-period, and activity-based quantities. Of the eight applications examined, only three explicitly and unambiguously state which reference quantity is used. Moreover, three corporate reports covering the same financial year delimit the respective cohort by different entry events. Neither of the two harmonization frameworks requires fleet aggregation. Additional gaps result from inconsistent temporal representation and a lack of alignment between foreground technologies and scenario-based background systems. Based on these findings, the synthesis identifies four alignment conditions, each accompanied by an indicator for detecting violations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Fleet-level pLCA is primarily constrained by methodological integration challenges rather than by the absence of suitable methods. Harmonization can be achieved by aligning existing approaches through clearer conceptual definitions, explicit temporal assumptions, and transparent documentation of scenario dependence, without introducing new assessment frameworks. The synthesis provides a methodological basis for the consistent operationalization of fleet-level pLCA in future applied studies and framework developments.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Environmental impact assessment of dairy protein from precision fermentation
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Precision fermentation (PF) has emerged as a promising approach to produce animal-free dairy proteins, yet its environmental performance remains insufficiently understood, particularly for consumer-ready products. This study quantifies the environmental impacts of a PF–based milk-like beverage (PF milk) in different scenarios and compares its impacts with cow’s milk and an oat-based drink. Results are reported per kilogram of final product at the point of consumption and per kilogram of protein powder (92% purity).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A cradle-to-consumer comparative LCA was conducted according to ISO 14040 in openLCA 2.4.1, comparing PF milk produced with recombinant beta-lactoglobulin, cow’s milk, and an oat-based drink. Impact assessment was based on EF 3.1, complemented by a biodiversity indicator linked to land use. Five electricity scenarios (European average, German, Polish, Norwegian, and 100% renewable) and two process-improvement scenarios were modelled. Comparative results across all scenarios are shown relative to cow’s milk.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Climate impacts of PF milk range from 0.64 kg CO
                      <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                      -eq/kg under low-carbon electricity to 1.29 kg CO
                      <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                      -eq/kg under fossil-intensive electricity mixes leading to a reduction of 10–55% compared to cow’s milk (1.44 kg CO
                      <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                      -eq/kg). Under the European average electricity mix, PF milk results in 0.86 kg CO
                      <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                      -eq/kg, which is 40% lower than cow’s milk and 76% higher than the oat-based drink (0.49 kg CO
                      <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                      -eq/kg). Fossil resource use of PF milk exceeds oat-based drink (7.52 MJ/kg) and cow’s milk (6.94 MJ/kg) across all scenarios, ranging from 8.09 to 15.57 MJ/kg (+ 17%–124% relative to cow’s milk). This is mainly driven by electricity demand during protein production and fossil resource use associated with formulation, packaging, and distribution. Compared to cow’s milk, land occupation is reduced by 60–68% and biodiversity impacts by 45–51%, largely irrespective of the electricity mix. Conversely, PF milk exhibits higher water-related impacts than both reference products in all scenarios, with volumetric water use exceeding cow’s milk by 402–878% (0.15–0.3 m³/kg) and scarcity-weighted water use by 65–354% (0.62–1.72 m³ world-eq/kg).
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Electricity supply, feedstock sourcing, formulation, and downstream logistics dominate the environmental performance of PF milk. PF milk substantially reduces land use and biodiversity pressures relative to dairy, whereas climate, fossil resource use, and water use impacts remain highly dependent on energy supply and process conditions. PF milk is thus best regarded as a context-specific complement to plant-based alternatives rather than a universal solution for sustainable food systems.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Uncertainty in LCA of emerging technologies: a systematic review
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) of emerging technologies involves great uncertainty due to limited data, technological pathway indeterminacy, and scale-up challenges. This systematic literature review examines how practitioners quantify and address uncertainty in LCA of emerging technologies, the limitations of current approaches, and their usefulness for supporting technology development and decision-making.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A systematic literature review following PRISMA guidelines was conducted using Scopus. Studies were eligible if they focused on emerging technologies and explicitly addressed uncertainty using parameter uncertainty, scenario analysis, and/or sensitivity analysis methods. Of 444 initial records identified, 230 peer-reviewed journal articles were included. Data extraction covered four categories: parameter uncertainty, scenario analysis, sensitivity analysis, and scale-up.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results and Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Of 230 studies, scenario analysis was applied in 211, sensitivity analysis in 193, parameter uncertainty in 94, and scale-up was addressed in 163. Methods frequently overlapped, reflecting both methodological flexibility and the different questions uncertainty assessment needs to answer. Probabilistic sampling dominated parameter uncertainty, but can create false precision when probability distributions cannot be meaningfully defined. Scenario analysis was particularly useful for exploring alternative technological pathways and future conditions, while sensitivity analysis can identify where further data collection or technology development is most valuable. Discrete sensitivity analysis was the most frequently applied sensitivity approach, although one-at-a-time methods can miss interactions and non-linearities. Scale-up further introduces uncertainty in both parameter values and technological configurations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The dominance of readily implemented methods does not necessarily reflect their suitability for emerging technologies. Probabilistic approaches remain appropriate for well-characterized parameters, but highly uncertain foreground data may require possibility-based or qualitative treatment. Scenario and sensitivity analyses are particularly valuable for technology development by comparing plausible pathways, identifying development priorities, and establishing decision thresholds. Practical guidance and software support for combining these approaches according to the available knowledge are needed.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: A framework for spatially explicit life cycle assessment based on application typologies: a case study on silicon metal production
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Spatially explicit Life Cycle Assessment aims to integrate the spatial context into the sustainability assessment, but limited standardization and software integration hinder its application in practice. This study proposes a framework that operationalizes spatialization through application typologies and demonstrates its use for Life Cycle Engineering, in the planning and sustainability analysis of industrial applications.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) is originally site-generic: spatial detail is typically aggregated, and location effects not propagated into impact results. However, spatial differentiation can occur through differences in the technosphere and biosphere. Silicon production, globally distributed among six major producing countries with varying conditions, provides a relevant example for the use of spatially explicit LCA. Through Brightway and LC-IMPACT, elementary flows can be spatially allocated to their emission locations, capturing both spatial distribution and magnitude of environmental impacts. Using application typologies, this framework separates the effects of technology implementation, upstream supply chains, and location-dependent ecosystem sensitivity. This helps identify impact hotspots and prioritize mitigation measures. It also reveals location-dependent outcomes, highlighting data and software gaps to guide future research.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results and discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Spatially-explicit attributes strongly influence LCA results for silicon production. Applying the proposed typologies shows that (i) under a technology focus LCA, shifting to biocarbon and decarbonized electricity allows decreasing silicon production net climate change effect by approximately half; (ii) under a background impact focus LCA, supply-chain hotspots emerge, notably land occupation in Brazil as a dominant charcoal supplier across countries; and (iii) under a foreground impact focus LCA, territorial sensitivity to plant locations becomes explicit, with the greatest vulnerability to water stress observed in China’s Xinjiang region. The main implementation challenge is that inventory databases often lack the geographical granularity needed to attribute upstream burdens to specific production locations. Another constraint is the limited availability of spatially explicit impact categories and methods in LCA software.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Because they address different questions, accounting for spatial variation in both the technosphere and biosphere is essential for Life Cycle Engineering, without neglecting supply chain impacts and where these occur. Although this study examined different focus areas separately, a holistic implementation that integrates technology, foreground, and background dimensions is ultimately required to capture interrelated effects and support more robust mitigation decisions. Future research should target the gaps identified in this article to enable such integrated assessments.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Artificial intelligence meets LCA: a critical analysis from technical, ethical, and organizational perspectives
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Artificial intelligence (AI) holds strong potential to automate repetitive and data-intensive life cycle assessment (LCA) tasks, thereby reducing costs, enabling scalability, and improving data access. This study critically analyzes the integration of AI into LCA from technical, ethical, and organizational perspectives. It aims to evaluate how AI can be implemented across LCA workflow steps to enhance efficiency without compromising effectiveness, inclusivity, and core LCA ethical values such as transparency and scientific integrity.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We conducted a literature review to identify and characterize the technical approaches of current AI-LCA applications across academic research and commercial tools, complemented by a survey assessing current AI uptake in LCA practice and perceived ethical risks. Ethical risks, like accountability or fairness, were derived from existing AI ethical principles and analyzed for their potential conflict with LCA ethical values. Organizational implications including changes in work practices and regional disparities were explored, with attention to the role of AI in social LCA. Identified applications were critically assessed against four categories: technical maturity, potential to enhance LCA practices, operational feasibility, and ethical risks, and used to qualitatively derive criticality of ethical risks.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results and discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Most AI-LCA applications focus on predicting impact scores and estimating missing inventory data. Few are employing generative AI, while it is mainly used by practitioners for auxiliary tasks like compiling a literature review and report writing. Despite high automation potential, most publicly documented applications remain at proof-of-concept stage, and face operational barriers for inclusivity (coding skills, restricted access) resulting in low adoption. Most critical ethical risks relate to fairness, transparency, accountability and sustainability, driven by black-box models, poor documentation, and representation bias, threatening all core LCA values. Emerging commercial AI-LCA tools present a high potential to widen AI adoption in LCA, but present higher risks toward sustainability, transparency, safety and security. AI is expected to shift LCA stakeholders’ roles from manual tasks to supervising algorithms and validating outputs, while potentially reinforcing regional disparities due to unequal access to AI tools, data, and expertise.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>AI can significantly enhance LCA efficiency and scalability, but without robust collaborative governance, it may undermine methodological rigor and ethical principles. Responsible integration requires need-based adoption, standardized protocols for evaluating AI models in LCA context, human-in-command validation for value choices, transparent documentation, and proactive attention to fairness and inclusivity. These findings provide a foundation for guidance toward effective, inclusive, and responsible use of AI in LCA.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Climate change impacts of recurring office fit-outs: a prospective life cycle assessment of circular economy-based improvements
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Buildings with long service life are associated with recurring greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions arising from repeated activities such as refurbishments over time, which can significantly contribute to the cumulative climate change impact. In particular, multi-tenant office buildings, where fit-outs typically occur every 2–10 years, contribute approximately a quarter of GHG emissions over the building service life. This study applies prospective LCA (pLCA) to quantify the climate change impact over the service life of a tenanted office building and assesses the effect of circular economy (CE) strategies using time-differentiated analysis. In contrast to static life cycle assessment (LCA), this approach enables climate change impact assessment of future scenarios with changed processes to account for potential future emissions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Method</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      An office fit-out case study in Aotearoa New Zealand was modelled using attributional LCA. The climate change impact was initially quantified using static LCA and hotspots were identified for applying CE strategies. Alternative CE strategies were then modelled using static LCA, related to maximising reuse, design for optimisation, and using low-impact materials. Then pLCA was conducted using the
                      <jats:italic>premise</jats:italic>
                      software to quantify the future climate change impact by analysing office fit-outs across four subsequent fit-out cycles at 10-year intervals, with and without implementation of CE strategies. In addition to the global future scenarios in
                      <jats:italic>premise</jats:italic>
                      , a national electricity decarbonisation pathway was included in the scenario modelling. Sensitivity analyses were conducted to assess the robustness to key assumptions in the evaluated CE strategies and use of alternative climate policy pathways.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results and discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The static LCA results showed that office fit-outs in module B5 are dominated by GHG emissions arising from manufacture of materials and components. Implementing all the evaluated CE strategies can reduce the net climate change impact of a single office fit-out - modelled using static LCA - by 17%. However, when modelled using pLCA, the net climate change impact of the final office fit-out is reduced by 56% relative to the same office fit-out modelled using static LCA.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study shows that pLCA enables a more comprehensive evaluation of future GHG emissions associated with recurring fit-outs in office buildings, and the future mitigation potential of CE strategies that target current GHG emission hotspots. Through the incorporation of prospective background data, the results capture potential future technological, socio-economic, and climate policy developments that are not represented in static LCA.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Developing willingness-to-pay-based effect factors for marine cultural ecosystem services in life cycle impact assessment
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Cultural ecosystem services (CES) are absent from current Life Cycle Impact Assessment (LCIA) methods. This study investigates the use of willingness-to-pay as a basis for deriving monetary effect factors (EFs) for marine CES affected by macroplastics. To our knowledge, this study provides the first set of spatialized EFs for marine CES impacts, demonstrating how willingness-to-pay (WTP) can quantify impact on CES within the LCIA framework.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Monetary EFs were developed based on an European WTP survey on marine plastic removal in eight countries, additional 13 countries´ WTP were extrapolated using disposable income. Coupled with marine plastic burden in each country, the resulting 21 national EFs express the potential loss of holistic cultural utility per unit of stranded macroplastics in [€/kg] and [€/item]. The mass of an average stranded plastic item is derived from each countries’ beach cleanup results. The dual units ensure compatibility with life cycle inventories. A case application in the Froan Archipelago (Norway) illustrates the relevance of the EFs and their role in the LCIA cause–effect chain, linking plastics stress to CES loss.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results and discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The WTP-based EFs enable the quantification of CES impacts in monetary terms consistent with existing LCA monetization. National EFs varied greatly, ranging from 233 €/kg to 1,730,000 €/kg by mass and 7.41€/item to 74,200 €/item by item count. The population-weighted averages for Europe were 65,200 €/kg and 5,310 €/item, respectively. This variability was driven mainly by differences in estimated stranded plastic burden, while WTP differences, reflecting economic and cultural contexts, contributed to a smaller extent. Incorporating WTP-based valuation offers a transferable means for integrating impacts on ecosystem services into LCIA.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study demonstrates that WTP provides a practical and conceptually coherent basis for quantifying CES impacts within LCIA. The proposed EFs represent an initial step toward monetized characterization factors for CES damages from macroplastics. The framework enhances the representation of ecosystem services in LCA and can be extended to other environmental stressors and geographic contexts.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Life cycle sustainability assessment–driven circular implementation framework for the textile industry
Rebound effects in food-system life cycle assessments: insights from practitioners
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Demand-side interventions, including food waste prevention, are widely promoted as means to reduce the environmental impacts of food systems. Life Cycle Assessment is central to quantifying these benefits, yet assessments often rely on substitution assumptions, while other behavioural and economic responses remain weakly addressed. This study examines how Life Cycle Assessment practitioners understand, consider, and address rebound effects in food-system assessments, using food-waste prevention as a salient example.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      An online survey was conducted among Life Cycle Assessment practitioners working with food-system and food-waste-related assessments (
                      <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                       = 79). The survey combined quantitative questions on familiarity, perceived importance, and current practice with open-ended questions capturing motivations, barriers, and reasoning. Quantitative responses were analysed descriptively, and qualitative responses were analysed thematically to identify recurring patterns and explanatory themes.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results and discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Rebound effects were rated as moderately important but were rarely included in quantitative modelling. Practitioners did not exclude rebound effects because they were considered irrelevant, but because conditions for credible inclusion were often lacking, including data limitations, high uncertainty, limited procedural guidance, and insufficient interdisciplinary capacity. In contrast, substitution assumptions implemented via system expansion are routinely applied despite comparable uncertainty. This suggests an asymmetric treatment of substitution assumptions and rebound effects in applied food-system Life Cycle Assessment practice, where uncertainty functions as a selective gatekeeper rather than a consistent criterion for inclusion or exclusion.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings indicate a structural misalignment between the recognised relevance of rebound effects and their practical treatment in food-system Life Cycle Assessments. Addressing this misalignment requires clearer methodological guidance on how rebound mechanisms relate to commonly applied substitution assumptions and how uncertainty can be handled more consistently when Life Cycle Assessment is used to inform food-system policies, mitigation targets, and intervention prioritisation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Towards greater sensitivity: advancing social life cycle assessment for the coffee sector in Brazil and the Democratic Republic of the Congo
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Literature on coffee sustainability focuses on environmental and economic challenges and often falls short on social factors that strongly influence overall sustainability. For coffee producers, social aspects are existentially important, while environmental concerns take lower priority. Recognizing that social aspects are critical to sustainable development, we assessed the social impacts of nine coffee case studies in Brazil and the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Social Life Cycle Assessment (S-LCA) has gained interest and importance to better understand and measure the positive and negative social impacts of products on various stakeholders. However, many challenges in its applicability still exist. Therefore, in this study, we operationalized and applied the S-LCA methodology for the coffee sector, based on the UNEP guidelines and the ISO standard 14,075. We used the reference scale approach based only on primary, site-specific data and systematically involved different actors at the upstream stages of the coffee value chain to capture multiple perspectives. In total, we conducted 170 inventory interviews and included six validation interviews.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We found significant differences in social performance both within and across the two countries; cross-country differences are reported to contrast the two contexts rather than to rank performance. The differences we found within the two countries show that not only context but also organization matters. Especially in Brazil, the cooperative models scored higher than the commercial plantations. In the Brazilian case studies, mean performance scores were highest for the stakeholder category ‘farmer’, followed by ‘local community’, ‘worker’, and ‘value chain actors’. In the Congolese case studies, mean performance scores were highest for the stakeholder category ‘local community’, followed by ‘farmer’, ‘worker’, and ‘value chain actors’. The impact subcategories showing the lowest social performance scores, such as ‘fair salary’, ‘livelihood and well-being’, and ‘productivity’, are the ones that were ranked highest during the validation interviews. We found that workers mostly do not earn living wages, with only seven exceptions in Brazil and one in the DRC.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study contributes to the limited body of S-LCA research on coffee production, and, to our knowledge, is among the first to be based on primary data collected in Brazil and the DRC. It presents a novel approach for achieving greater case sensitivity in S-LCA through primary data and context-specific reference scales, going beyond generic databases. This approach makes it possible to account for differences among case studies within the same country and sector.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Comparative life cycle assessment: environmental impact of beef jerky and its plant-based analogue
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Rising population, income, and urbanisation are increasing demand for animal protein, intensifying environmental pressures associated with meat production. This study evaluates the environmental performance of a plant-based jerky analogue compared with conventional beef jerky, assessing whether a product derived from plant protein blends via high-moisture extrusion can reduce impacts across multiple environmental impact categories.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A cradle-to-gate life cycle assessment (LCA) was performed using the Environmental Footprint 3.1 method to compare beef jerky with a plant-based jerky analogue derived from a plant protein blend. System boundaries covered raw material production, processing, and packaging. The beef jerky inventory was compiled from scientific literature, while primary data from the manufacturer were used for the plant-based product. Background data were sourced from ecoinvent v3.10, Agri-Footprint v6.3, and AGRIBALYSE v3.1 databases. Environmental impacts were assessed across 16 impact categories for two functional units: 1 kg of product and 1 kg of protein. Contribution analysis identified key drivers, and sensitivity and uncertainty analysis evaluated the robustness of the results.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results and discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Plant-based jerky showed lower environmental impacts in 15 out of 16 categories for both functional units, with ionising radiation being the only exception. On a product basis, reductions reached 95.0% for climate change and 49.0% for water use. The land-use impact for the plant-based product was negative, which was attributed to the selected characterization method rather than treating it as an absolute environmental benefit. Raw material production was the dominant contributor in both systems. For beef jerky, livestock production drove most impacts, while crop cultivation and protein extraction were the main contributors for the plant-based alternative. Results remained consistent under different sensitivity assessments, confirming robustness. Additional processing stages did not offset the overall environmental advantages of the plant-based product.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The plant-based jerky demonstrates substantially lower environmental impacts than beef jerky across most impact categories, indicating strong potential as a more sustainable alternative. In both systems, raw material production dominates environmental burdens, highlighting the need for targeted upstream improvements to achieve further reductions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Recommendations</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Future research should evaluate the combined usage of multiple plant protein sources and account for the cumulative impacts of additional processing stages. Comparative assessments should also incorporate nutritional factors, including protein digestibility, bioavailability, and conversion efficiency, to enable a more comprehensive evaluation of plant- and animal-based products.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Revisiting microbial supply assumptions: implications of boundary definition for life cycle assessment of bioleaching systems
Consequential life cycle assessment of agricultural products: state of the art and research needs
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Consequential Life Cycle Assessment (cLCA) was developed to assess large-scale consequences, supporting applications like policy-making. Unlike the well-established attributional approach, cLCA is characterized by lower maturity. Specifically, a lack of consensus on the identification of marginal data, system boundary setting and handling of results’ uncertainties impedes its practical use. We examine how agricultural cLCA studies handle these methodological challenges, focusing on food and biobased materials.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A systematic literature review was carried out, initially yielding 229 cLCA studies. The eligibility screening led to the final selection of 23 studies on biobased materials and 32 studies on food. These were primarily analysed regarding marginal data identification, system boundary setting, and uncertainty assessment, alongside supplementary methodological aspects, such as functional unit, use of market models, study scope, and reasoning for consequential modelling.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results and Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The review identified a broad variety of approaches for addressing methodological challenges of cLCA, without significant differences between biobased materials and food, while revealing documentation gaps and inconsistencies in reported methodological procedures. Marginal data identification relied mostly on ecoinvent consequential and formalized guidelines, while 11% of the studies did not specify the procedure. Around a third reported using market models or projections. System boundary setting was generally well documented, yet often lacked details, raising concerns regarding the completeness of captured changes. For uncertainty, 25% applied statistical methods and 62% conducted at least a sensitivity analysis, while 22% relied on qualitative discussion only. Further observations included the absence of specifications for temporal scope and justification for consequential modelling.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions and Recommendations</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To improve robustness, cLCA studies would benefit from standardized minimum procedural requirements, for which suggestions from this review can be viewed as a starting point. Specifically, we recommend i) using the JRC (2010) classification as a checklist to qualitatively discuss potential secondary consequences, ii) conducting sensitivity analysis, and iii) explicitly defining the temporal scope. Increased application of quantitative uncertainty assessment would strengthen the reliability of cLCA studies.</jats:p>
                    <jats:p> Future research could test these suggestions in case studies, examine marginal data identification with respect to the practical applicability of existing procedures, and expand the review to biofuels. Overall, methodological harmonization and transparent study documentation are key to increasing the reliability and broader acceptance of cLCA.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Advancing silicon die area estimation for integrated circuit modeling in life-cycle assessments
Development of environmental footprint product category rules for Finnish food sector in alignment with Product Environmental Footprint (PEF) method
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aimed to address the pressing need for harmonised life cycle assessment (LCA) practices in the food sector by developing methods that enable comparable, accessible, acceptable, and applicable environmental footprint assessments of food products. Specifically, the study reviewed existing LCA guidelines and Product Environmental Footprint Category Rules (PEFCRs), which were used as a basis to formulate comprehensive methodological guidance for the external communication of environmental information about food products marketed in Finland.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To support the development of methodological guidance for assessing the environmental footprint of food products in the Finnish market, the relevant scientific literature, LCA standards and reports, and policy documents were reviewed. The methods’ adoptability and practical applicability were further assessed based on their data requirements and through consultations with key stakeholders for accessibility and acceptability. Particular attention was paid to four impact categories, climate change, water use, and freshwater, and marine eutrophication, in both the harmonisation of LCA methodologies and the formulation of Finnish Food LCA guidance.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results and discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Through the methodological review and stakeholder consultations, several inconsistencies, inapplicability, and accessibility issues were identified in the Product Environmental Footprint (PEF) and PEFCR methods, which were subsequently harmonised for the overall Food LCA guidance. Key adjustments included selecting accessible methods for greenhouse gas (GHG) and land use and land use change (LULUC) emissions, omitting circular footprint formula (CFF) due to its complexity and deviation from the attributional approach, recommending only economic allocation, replacing the functional unit with the declared unit to ensure applicability across all food products, clarifying water scarcity and eutrophication assessment, and including an approach for eutrophication assessment in Baltic Sea conditions, and providing detailed guidance on peat modelling.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study identified several inconsistencies in current approaches and highlighted broader development needs for enhancing the harmonisation of food LCAs and the European Commission’s PEF method, including needs for standardised methods for animal production emissions, improved modelling of soil carbon, crop sequences, and organic fertilisers, region-specific eutrophication models, integration of social and economic sustainability dimensions, and clear guidance on the inclusion of nutritional aspects to enable fair product comparisons while avoiding greenwashing.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Environmental evaluation of plastic waste end-of-life pathways in Malang District, Indonesia: a life cycle approach
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Malang is an Indonesian District struggling with waste management: low collection rates, fly-tipping, and burning. This study conducts a Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) on the end-of-life pathways of plastic waste (PW) in Malang. All the stages of the PW management system are covered, from PW generation and transportation to unregulated and regulated PW management strategies. Ultimately, the findings aim to support policymakers in understanding the environmental impact of PW management and how to mitigate it.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Stakeholder interviews provided primary data, which informed the Life Cycle Inventory (LCI) across all stages of the PW management system in villages of Malang District. The data was then adapted into the functional unit (FU) of 1 kg of PW generated and statistically analysed to understand PW end-of-life trends. The LCA was conducted using the open-source software Activity Browser. In this case, the ReCiPe v1.03 midpoint impact categories considered were global warming, primary energy depletion, and particulate matter formation. The results of the analysed villages were compared with the national average. The PW from four villages (Bakalan, Krebet Senggrong, Krebet, and Tlogorejo) were modelled under three end-of-life scenarios i.e., landfilling, recycling, and incineration with energy recovery to inform intervention selection.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results and discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In the baseline scenarios of the villages, the highest impact in Global Warming Potential, Fossil Fuel Potential, and Particulate Matter Formation Potential (GWP100, FFP, and PMFP, respectively) was linked to higher rates of open burning (e.g., Krebet Senggrong where 35% of waste is open burned). Villages with the highest recycling rates however present lower GWP100 and FFP, such as the case of Bedali and Mangunrejo, where 16.6% and 14.3% of plastic is recycled, respectively. Low PMFP is tied to options such as landfilling, which occurred in Rekasan. The alternative intervention strategy with the lowest environmental impact is recycling (when considering avoided plastic production, GWP100 and FFP are negative). However, it is the alternative with the highest PMFP, even surpassing the baseline scenario.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Open burning remains one of the most prevalent PW management strategies in Malang, which is not only detrimental to the environment but also proven to negatively impact human health, particularly respiratory health. It is essential not only to increase waste collection and treatment rates, but also to ensure that waste‑management practices meet environmental standards and minimise adverse impacts on human health and the environment.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Assessment of GHG emission reduction potential of an integrated community solar and biogas renewable energy system: a case study of Hakwata Green Village in Zimbabwe
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study analyses the greenhouse gas (GHG) emission impact of a combined community solar and biogas energy system, using the Hakwata Green Village in Zimbabwe as a case study. The primary aim is to evaluate the Global Warming Potential (GWP) reduction for carbon finance achieved by a 200 kWp/915 kWh solar mini-grid and a 540 m³ biogas plant serving over 12 500 people, relative to default alternatives (grid extension for solar; firewood for biogas).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A comprehensive Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) was conducted using SimaPro with the ReCiPe 2016 method, focusing on GWP as the key climate change driver and role in carbon finance. The study employs a dual functional unit system: kWh of electricity delivered from the solar mini grid and MJ of energy delivered from the biogas system over the project’s 20-year life. Avoided emissions were calculated from the replacement of national grid with solar, firewood with biogas and the replacement of synthetic fertiliser with biogas digestate.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results and discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The solar PV system exhibits a life-cycle emission intensity of 145 g CO₂ eq kWh⁻¹, an 85% reduction compared to the Southern African Power Pool grid (SAPP) mix (980 g CO₂ eq kWh⁻¹). The biogas system, despite construction phase emissions, achieves a net negative carbon balance of 26,851.90 t CO₂ eq over 20 years once avoided firewood and synthetic fertiliser burdens are credited. When the two subsystems are combined and compared with the baseline, the integrated community energy system reduces GWP by 1,614 t CO₂ eq year⁻¹, yielding a cumulative net reduction of 33,408 t CO₂ eq over the 20-year project life.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings confirm that an integrated solar-biogas community energy system can deliver emission reductions of 8% against grid electricity and 9% against firewood, while avoiding 33,408 t CO₂ eq over 20 years. These verified reductions, combined with improved energy access, make such projects are strong candidates for carbon finance, offering a replicable rural electrification model beyond the Hakwata Green Village case.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Interoperability of uncertainty information in LCI databases
A global consensus life cycle impact assessment method - GLAM: impacts on ecosystem quality
Transparent and harmonized allocation factors for crop-processing co-products in U.S. dairy rations
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Crop-processing co-products are widely used in U.S. dairy rations and contribute substantially to feed supply, yet the allocation factors needed to assign them a share of upstream crop-production burdens are not harmonized across methods or available in a single transparent resource.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study compiled a database of economic, dry-matter mass, and gross energy allocation factors for 62 dairy-relevant co-products from 22 U.S. plant-processing systems, including small grains, oilseeds, sugar crops, vegetables, and specialty crops, derived from explicit equations applied to harmonized inventory data for 2024–2025. Parametric uncertainty was quantified using Monte Carlo simulation with 10,000 iterations per system and Program Evaluation and Review Technique (PERT) distributed inputs for co-product yields, market prices, and gross energy content, and a cross-method divergence index was used to characterize sensitivity to allocation choice.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results and discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Of the 62 co-products evaluated, 29 were classified as high sensitivity, 22 as moderate, and 11 as low, with the greatest divergence occurring in almond, sweet corn, citrus, peanut, cotton, and safflower systems. For most co-products, variation across allocation methods exceeded parametric uncertainty within any single method, indicating that allocation choice is the main source of methodological variability in co-product environmental assessment.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The resulting factors are impact-category neutral and designed to interface with any upstream crop life-cycle inventory, complementing rather than replacing allocations already embedded in general-purpose life-cycle inventory databases.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Consensus-based framework for the impact assessment of natural resource use in life cycle assessment: generalized impact pathways and recommended methods for abiotic resource use
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aimed to establish a consistent framework for assessing the impacts of natural resource use within Life Cycle Assessment (LCA). As part of the outcomes of the UNEP Life Cycle Initiative’s GLAM Phase 3 Task Force on Natural Resources, the work defines the safeguard subject, generalized impact pathways applicable across all types of natural resources, and recommended methods for abiotic resource use that aligns with the developed assessment framework for natural resources.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>An expert consensus was achieved through a structured evaluation of twenty existing methods using ten criteria, including relevance to the defined safeguard subject, consistency with impact pathways, data quality, and compatibility with Life Cycle Inventory (LCI) databases. The generalized impact pathways were developed to encompass abiotic, biotic and other renewable resources, integrating mechanisms such as dissipation, degradation, and occupation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The consensus-building process resulted in the definition of a common safeguard subject for natural resource use: the potential to make use of the instrumental values of natural resources. Generalized impact pathways were established to consistently describe cause-effect mechanisms across different categories of natural resources. The Future Welfare Loss (FWL) model was selected as the recommended approach for assessing mineral and fossil resource use. Characterization factors (CFs) were recalculated using updated 2018 commodity price data for 81 minerals, 3 fossil resources, and 2 energy carriers. The global annual impact of mineral and fossil resource use (using extraction flows as inputs) was estimated at approximately USD 3,483 billion, equivalent to about 4% of the 2018 global GDP.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>While the generalized impact pathways are intended to be broadly applicable across natural resource categories, the operational recommendation and updated characterization factors currently focus on mineral and fossil resource use, whereas only interim recommendations could be identified for water resource use and land use assessment. Further methodological refinement is needed for renewable resources. Finally, we encourage LCI databases developers to improve the coverage of mineral and fossil resource dissipative flows in LCI databases to enhance the characterization of resource dissipation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Carbon footprint and carbon-related costs of LFP and NMC811 traction battery packs in China – a pack-level life-cycle assessment under trade-weighted carbon price exposure
Appetite-based functional units for food life cycle assessment: integrating experimental measures of satiety and satiation
Leveraging life cycle assessment for biodiversity footprint: application to renewable energy technologies and lessons learned
A lifecycle perspective to environmental and social impacts of electric vehicle batteries: a literature review
A V-model for LCA: scheduling life cycle assessment within product development
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>As of today, Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) is a process that is still largely separated from product development processes. Acknowledging the increasing necessity for sustainable product development amidst stringent regulatory and consumer demands, integration of LCA into product development processes is necessary to ensure efficient ecodesign practices.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In this paper a methodology integrating Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) into methods of product development, specifically the V-model is used to schedule LCA in product development processes. The methodology identifies critical data needs and sources relevant to LCA, ensuring a scheduled integration of sustainability metrics into the existing V-model for product development. A V-model structure for LCA studies is provided to emphasize the similarities between LCA and product development processes. A clustered assessment strategy is introduced, segmenting the LCA into partial assessment based on life cycle stages and respective data needs in the development process. A case study for the development of a rotor of an electric motor is conducted to exemplify the implications of the methodology.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The resulting V-model-based methodology for scheduling LCA within product development presents a novel approach that uses the product development process itself as the basis for LCA integration, explicitly addressing the temporal dimension and enabling early, cluster-specific assessments along the product development process. The V-model for LCA presents a step towards LCA-centred product development processes, aligning the two procedures by splitting LCA into three clusters based on development steps. The case study partially shows the applicability of the scheduled application of LCA during product development for two of the three clusters. Hotspots for the design of the developed rotor for an electric motor in the impact category climate change were identified in the raw material acquisition stage, especially the magnets (about 91% of impact).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>By providing a methodology for the integration of LCA in the V-model, the study supports practitioners in making informed decisions that reflect environmental impacts, ultimately contributing to more sustainable designs. The conducted work contributes to the advancement of ecodesign frameworks by merging LCA with established product development processes as described in VDI/VDE 2206, thereby fostering a holistic approach to sustainable innovation. It thus contributes to the advancement in process oriented LCA frameworks.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: The overlooked impact of materials’ reference service life on the whole-building life cycle assessment results
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Life cycle assessment (LCA) offers a robust framework for evaluating the environmental impacts of a building throughout its entire life cycle, from material extraction to end-of-life. A key source of uncertainty in LCA is the reference service life (RSL) of building materials, particularly non-structural components, which are often overlooked compared to structural elements. This study aims to examine how the RSL of non-structural materials influences the LCA results of different building types.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study addresses this objective by developing a RSL database for non-structural building materials, based on North American Environmental Product Declarations (EPDs). It prioritizes components that exhibit high variability and explicitly considers their RSL in LCA calculations, which are frequently ignored or replaced with default values in detailed LCA modeling. The database was applied to three representative residential building architypes, single-family (SF), row house (RH), and multi-unit residential building (MURB), assuming a 75-year lifespan as the baseline and varying it between 60 and 90 years. Material quantities for the SF and RH models were obtained from detailed BIM models, while the MURB model used standard quantities from a bill of materials (BOM).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results and discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The results reveal that underestimating the RSL of a single high-impact component can significantly alter embodied greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions in the B4 module. For example, assuming the highest replacement rates for the non–structural materials increase total LCA results by 35–37% for SF and RH buildings, and by approximately 19% for MURB. Moreover, extending building lifespan from 60 to 90 years can further change wbLCA results increased by about 47% and 58% for SF and RH, and 23% for MURB.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>These findings highlight the critical need for accurate and standardized RSL data. It is recommended that policymakers require the inclusion of verified RSLs in EPDs, supported by product-specific testing or modeling. Additionally, the development of region-specific, open-access RSL databases would help reduce uncertainty, improve comparability, and ultimately enable more accurate assessments and reliable life cycle-based decision-making.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: The nuts and bolts of publishing in the International Journal of Life Cycle Assessment
A Global Consensus Life Cycle Impact Assessment Method (GLAM): impacts on human health
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Millions of humans worldwide die prematurely or live with reduced quality of life, partly attributable to pollutant emissions along product, service and technology life cycles, including greenhouse gas emissions, and exposure to air pollutants and toxic chemicals. However, while many of these factors are considered in currently available life cycle impact assessment (LCIA) methods, other aspects affecting human health as a central area of protection in LCIA are currently incomplete or missing. This includes impacts in occupational environments and nutrition-related impacts.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      The Global Life Cycle Impact Assessment Method (GLAM) was developed as a comprehensive and consensus-driven LCIA method, with methodological documentation and guidance on GLAM human health impact categories provided in the present study. For human health, GLAM proposes indicators for climate change, fine particulate matter (PM
                      <jats:sub>2.5</jats:sub>
                      ) impacts, human toxicity and ionizing radiation that are also available in other LCIA methods as well as for work environment impacts, water scarcity impacts, and lifestyle impacts related to nutrition and physical activity as novel impact categories.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Beyond the introduction of new impact categories, GLAM provides innovation related to differentiating short- and long-term climate change impacts, exposure to indoor and spatialized outdoor PM
                      <jats:sub>2.5</jats:sub>
                      sources, coupling exposure from chemical life cycle emissions and chemicals in products and introducing reproductive/developmental effects for human toxicity, and building on the Global Burden of Disease (GBD) study series for the exposure-response and severity assessment across most considered impact categories. GLAM version 1 was released publicly end of 2024.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>While GLAM impact characterization factors can be used in life cycle assessment and environmental footprinting, they still require extensive testing in practical studies. GLAM ultimately contributes to achieving health-related targets set in the United Nations’ Sustainable Development Goals as well as in the Global Framework on Chemicals.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Would you eat horse? A life cycle assessment of horsemeat from end-of-life horses, produced in the Americas and consumed in Europe
Herbal residue treatment and return-to-field application: life cycle assessment combined with economic, thermodynamic, and ecological analysis
Nature-based solutions in aquaculture: a sustainability assessment of tilapia monoculture and tilapia-shrimp polyculture
Racial discrimination in social life cycle assessment: indicators and reference scales
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Racial discrimination remains a pervasive social issue but is not systematically addressed in current social life cycle assessment (S-LCA) frameworks. Existing guidelines cover general discrimination only under the subcategory
                      <jats:italic>equal opportunities/discrimination</jats:italic>
                      for the stakeholder group
                      <jats:italic>worker</jats:italic>
                      , which is insufficient, as racial discrimination can occur across supply chains and affect multiple stakeholder groups.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study reviewed S-LCA guiding documents and databases to assess current coverage and to identify gaps. Based on these findings and incorporation of interdisciplinary evidence on racial discrimination from e.g., labour psychology and healthcare, indicators were developed for workers, value chain actors, local communities, and children. They were then reviewed by international racism experts and adapted based on their feedback.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results and discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>38 expert-reviewed indicators assessing racial discrimination in S-LCA were proposed and grouped into two sets: a core set representing minimum compliance with anti-racist practices and an advanced set incorporating aspirational measures aimed at addressing systemic racism. A set of reference scales was developed to facilitate implementation for practitioners. The set can be adapted to specific systems under study and local contexts. Methodological and practical challenges remain, including survey design, site-specific data availability, and risks of underreporting.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This work provides the first comprehensive framework for integrating racial discrimination into S-LCA using the reference scale approach and highlights the central role of organisations in addressing racial inequities across supply chains. Next steps include the testing and optimisation of the reference scales in practical application across various sectors and geographical contexts. Future work should expand this foundational work and cover racial discrimination within the impact pathway approach.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
